title: Frame Control — 10 Rules
description: A self-test on the 10 rules of frame control. Includes recall questions, scenario applications, and edge-case traps.

tests.title: Rule Recall
tests.instructions: Match the rule number or name.

questions.prompt: Which rule says: pause one beat longer than the conversation expects?
options: Slow Your Responses
Use Strategic Silence
Stay in Your Own Mood
Be Willing to Walk

questions.prompt: What does Rule 2 (Quit Over-Explaining) frame loss look like?
options: She makes a crack and you launch into backstory
You talk louder to be heard
You change the subject completely
You walk away mid-conversation

questions.prompt: Rule 3 says: stay in your own mood. What does 'catching the testy' mean?
options: Letting someone else's bad mood pull you out of your own
Testing whether someone is trustworthy
Getting caught in a lie
Having strong opinions about something

questions.prompt: According to Rule 4, what are the 'load-bearing walls of a frame'?
options: Opinions
Silence
Confidence
Experience

questions.prompt: Rule 5 — 'Be Willing to Walk' — says the deepest source of frame is:
options: The bone-level knowledge that you do not need this to go well
Having more money and status than the other person
Being physically larger and louder
Having prepared arguments for every counterpoint

questions.prompt: Which rule says: 'Not every challenge deserves a response'?
options: Use Strategic Silence
Slow Your Responses
Quit Over-Explaining
Know Your Standards

questions.prompt: Rule 7 ('Make Decisions Like a Leader') says that small leadership moments do what?
options: Compound into respect
Make people obey you
Replace the need for rules 1-6
Only work in professional settings

questions.prompt: According to Rule 8, frame is proactive, not reactive. This means:
options: State standards early, enforce them calmly
Wait for someone to cross a line first, then react
Assume everyone already knows your boundaries
Let violations slide the first time

questions.prompt: Rule 9 says 'Don't Negotiate Self-Respect.' What does it say about attraction without respect?
options: It is short-term
It is the most common kind
It can grow into respect over time
It's the same thing

questions.prompt: When you slip and lose frame (Rule 10), what should you do?
options: Acknowledge it internally, don't dwell, return to center
Grovel and apologize to repair the frame
Double down and act like it didn't happen
End the interaction entirely

tests.title: Scenario Drills
tests.instructions: Read each scenario and pick the response that best applies the rules.

questions.prompt: You're on a date. She says, 'You're kind of quiet tonight.' You feel the pull to explain — long day at work, tired, introverted, etc. Which response uses Rule 1 (Slow Your Responses) and Rule 2 (Quit Over-Explaining)?
options: Smile, pause a beat, say 'I'm right here,' and keep the evening moving
'Sorry, I'm just tired, work was brutal today, my boss...'
'Quiet? I'm not quiet, I was just listening to you'
Change the subject to something you're passionate about

questions.prompt: You're in a good mood. A coworker walks in visibly annoyed and starts sighing loudly, slamming drawers. You feel yourself starting to tense up. What does Rule 3 say?
options: Stay in your own lane — don't catch the testy
Match their energy so they feel understood
Ask them what's wrong and try to fix it
Leave the room until they calm down

questions.prompt: You're out with a group. Someone asks where you want to eat. Everyone says 'I don't know, wherever.' What does Rule 7 say to do?
options: Pick a place and say 'Let's go to [place]'
Keep asking until someone else decides
Suggest three options and let the group vote
Say 'I don't care either' to avoid conflict

questions.prompt: You and a partner are in a disagreement. She says something disrespectful — raises her voice, calls you a name. You feel your frame crack. Which combination of rules applies here?
options: Rule 8 (state standard calmly) + Rule 9 (don't negotiate respect) + Rule 5 (willing to walk)
Rule 2 (explain why it hurt you) + Rule 7 (decide how to fix it)
Rule 1 (pause) + Rule 6 (silence) — wait for her to apologize
Rule 4 (state your opinion about her behavior) + Rule 10 (acknowledge you slipped)

questions.prompt: She texts you: 'You're so full of yourself.' You were having a good day. What combination of rules handles this best?
options: Rule 3 — don't catch her testy mood
Rule 5 — be willing to walk (you don't need this to go well)
Rule 2 — explain that you didn't mean it that way
Rule 6 — not every challenge deserves a response
Rule 1 — pause before replying

questions.prompt: First date. She asks what you think about a movie you haven't seen. Which response best applies Rule 4 (Have Actual Opinions)?
options: 'I haven't seen it yet, but I generally like [director/genre]. What did you think of the ending?'
'I haven't seen it, sorry, I don't have an opinion'
'I'm sure it's fine, I'd watch anything really'
Lie and say you've seen it

questions.prompt: You made a mistake in a group setting and lost frame. People noticed. What does Rule 10 say to do?
options: Acknowledge it internally, don't dwell, return to center. Consistency over time rebuilds frame.
Apologize profusely and explain how it happened
Joke about it to deflect the awkwardness
Leave the situation entirely and try again tomorrow

questions.prompt: You've been dating someone for a month. She cancels last minute for the third time. What's the best application of Rule 8 (Know Your Standards) + Rule 5 (Willing to Walk)?
options: 'I value reliability in my connections. If plans change last minute three times, I'm going to take some space. I'll let you reach out when your schedule opens up.'
'It's fine, I understand things come up!'
'You always do this, why do I even bother?'
Stop responding entirely with no explanation

questions.prompt: In a conversation, she says something that could be interpreted as a slight or a joke. You're not sure which. Which rule applies most directly?
options: Rule 6 — Strategic Silence. Not every challenge deserves a response. Let it sit.
Rule 2 — ask for clarification to over-explain the situation
Rule 4 — state your opinion about what she said
Rule 7 — make a decision about how to interpret it

questions.prompt: You notice a pattern: every time someone challenges you, you talk more, go into detail, justify yourself. Which two rules do you need to internalize most?
options: Rule 1 — Slow Your Responses (pause first)
Rule 2 — Quit Over-Explaining (say less than you want to)
Rule 4 — Have Actual Opinions
Rule 7 — Make Decisions Like a Leader
Rule 6 — Strategic Silence

tests.title: Edge Cases & Traps
tests.instructions: These are harder. Multiple answers may seem right. Pick the BEST fit.

questions.prompt: Rule 1 says 'Slow Your Responses' and Rule 6 says 'Use Strategic Silence.' What's the difference?
options: Rule 1 is a pause before responding (you still answer). Rule 6 is choosing not to answer at all.
They are the same thing — silence is silence
Rule 1 is for arguments, Rule 6 is for flirting
Rule 1 is internal, Rule 6 is external
questions.rubric: Critical distinction. Rule 1 delays your response (you still engage, but on your beat). Rule 6 withholds a response entirely (some challenges don't deserve engagement).
questions.commonMistakes: Treating silence as one thing. Strategic silence is active non-engagement, not just delayed engagement.

questions.prompt: Rule 2 says 'Say less than you want to.' When should you IGNORE this rule?
options: When someone genuinely asks for your thoughts and the context calls for depth
Never — always say less than you want to
When you're angry and need to vent
When you feel the other person won't understand otherwise
questions.rubric: Rules aren't absolutes. Rule 2 guards against defensive over-explaining, not all explanation. Context matters.

questions.prompt: Rule 5 says 'Be Willing to Walk.' What's the difference between being willing to walk and actually walking?
options: Willingness to walk is an internal state (you don't need this). Actually walking is an action you take when standards are violated.
There is no difference — if you're willing to walk, you should walk
Being willing to walk means you threaten to leave; actually walking means you do it
Willingness to walk is a bluff; actually walking is real
questions.rubric: Key nuance. Willingness is posture (unshakeable because you don't need the outcome). Walking is the enforcement mechanism. You can hold the posture without acting on it.

questions.prompt: Rule 3 says 'Stay in Your Own Mood.' Your partner is clearly upset and needs support. If you stay in your own good mood, aren't you being cold?
options: Support and mood contagion are different. You can offer empathy without catching their emotional state.
Yes — you should match their mood to show you care
Rule 3 only applies to casual situations, not relationships
You should stay in your own mood but pretend to be upset
questions.rubric: Crucial distinction. Rule 3 is about not letting someone else's mood PULL you. Offering genuine support from a centered place is different from catching their chaos.

questions.prompt: Rule 9: 'Don't Negotiate Self-Respect.' You're in a long-term relationship. She crosses a boundary. You state your standard. She apologizes and asks for another chance. Is accepting that apology 'negotiating self-respect'?
options: No. Stating the standard and accepting a genuine apology is not negotiation — it's enforcement followed by grace.
Yes — you should walk permanently the first time any boundary is crossed
Only if the boundary was about respect specifically
It depends on how long you've been together
questions.rubric: Boundary enforcement doesn't mean zero forgiveness. The key is whether you stated the standard clearly and the apology was genuine — not whether you 'won' by staying mad.

questions.prompt: Rule 4 says have actual opinions. Which of these is an actual opinion vs. a preference vs. a non-opinion?
options: 'The pacing in the second act undermines the entire film' — opinion
'I like Italian food' — preference
'I don't know, whatever you want' — non-opinion
'That restaurant is great because of their wine list and the chef's technique' — opinion
'I don't have strong feelings about it' — acceptable non-opinion

questions.prompt: She's testing you by bringing up a topic she knows you disagree on (politics, religion, etc.). You feel your frame wobble. What's the play?
options: Rule 6 (silence doesn't mean you have no position) + Rule 4 (hold your opinion without needing to convert her) + Rule 5 (you don't need her agreement)
Rule 2 — explain your position thoroughly so she understands
Rule 7 — make a decision to avoid the topic entirely
Rule 3 — match her energy and engage fully
questions.rubric: Frame is tested most on high-stakes topics. Your position is: I know what I think, I don't need you to agree, and I'm not going to fight about it.

questions.prompt: You over-explained (violated Rule 2) and you feel the frame slip. What does Rule 10 actually say to do in this moment?
options: Acknowledge it internally, don't dwell, return to center right now
Verbally acknowledge the mistake to the other person
End the conversation and try again later
Over-explain why you over-explained (meta-apology)
questions.rubric: This is the most common trap. Meta-apologizing for frame loss is just more frame loss. The move: note it, drop it, come back to center.

tests.title: Written Reflection
tests.instructions: Answer honestly in your own words. There's no right answer — the goal is self-awareness.

questions.prompt: Which of the 10 rules do you struggle with most? Describe a specific situation where you lost frame and which rule would have helped.
Is there a person in your life who consistently pulls you out of your frame? Which rules would help you handle them differently?
Pick one rule to focus on for the next 7 days. How will you practice it? What's your specific trigger or cue to remember it?
